lines.text: Stick around for number six: a small change that helped people save almost four times more.
Brain scans point the same way. When people saw prices that felt too high, a brain region linked to pain and disgust became more active.
It even works with numbers that are obviously meaningless. People who first spun a wheel of fortune gave higher or lower estimates depending on where the wheel stopped.
Once you notice decoys, you see them everywhere: the very expensive wine on a menu that makes the second most expensive bottle look reasonable.
It also helps explain why someone might keep money in savings while paying high interest on a credit card. In their head, those are two separate jars.
The same thing happened with pens, and again when the researchers repeated the experiment.
And it isn't just money. When choosing a snack for right now, most people pick chocolate. When choosing for next week, most pick fruit.
A later study looked at more than one hundred countries. In most of them, people who had recently given money to charity were happier, in poorer and richer countries alike.
